A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, planning framework, and retained experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Maze2D experiments, a custom-environment comparison, and successful and failed trajectory examples.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds Cube, AntMaze, and predictor–generator–controller evaluations.

M1.justification: The three-stage planner, TimePredict model, and SafeDiffuser generator remain. However, the specified until decomposition changes invariance intervals from I(a, lambda, mu) to I(0, lambda, mu), with a corresponding correction for nested until (v1 Section 3.2; v2 Appendix D). These are localized procedural corrections; trajectory stitching already existed in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds OGBench AntMaze quadruped locomotion and Cube robotic-arm end-effector motion to the retained Maze2D and custom environments. These substantially broaden the evaluated dynamics and spatial coverage. Cube evaluates Cartesian waypoint motion, rather than object manipulation (Sections 5.2 and F.4).

E2.justification: The comparator membership remains RGD for Maze2D and the optimization-based method attributed to Gilpin et al. for the custom environment. The new Cube, AntMaze, and pipeline tables report only the proposed framework; newly cited methods are not added experimental baselines.

E3.justification: v2 introduces average robustness evaluation, 100 tasks per template in each new domain, and a separate 1,000-start–goal-pair protocol per environment. AntMaze uses two control updates per planning step. The retained Maze2D and custom experiments keep their 150 and 200 tasks per template, respectively, and their previously listed parameters.

E4.justification: New Appendix F.6 tests whether predicted travel times, generated segments, and execution control work together on sampled start–goal pairs. This is a targeted additional pipeline analysis, rather than a component ablation. The earlier custom allocator evaluation and qualitative failure analysis remain.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies runtime dispersion as standard deviation and specifies discarding the top and bottom 5% when estimating average robustness (Appendix F.3). v1 already reported runtime values with ± dispersion. Neither version reports experimental seed counts or repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: All shared numerical entries in the Maze2D and custom-environment tables are unchanged. v2 adds robustness scores, Cube success rates of 84–100% and AntMaze rates of 60–94% (Table F.3), and pipeline success rates of 93.9/89.0/83.7/84.8% across U-Maze/Medium/Large/AntMaze (Table F.5). These are additional results, not same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v1 has no formal soundness lemmas or proofs. v2 introduces feasible-assignment definitions, decomposition and allocation lemmas, an overall conditional soundness theorem, and proofs in Appendix G. Appendix D also corrects until intervals and formalizes independent variable copies for nested always decomposition.

C1.justification: The zero-shot planning contribution remains, but v2 adds formal STL-satisfaction guarantees as a central abstract, introduction, and conclusion claim. Its conclusion also expands the empirical contribution to more complex robotic dynamics and higher robustness values. The formal theorem conditions satisfaction on successful allocation and constraint-compliant generation.

C2.justification: New Appendix B substantially develops incompleteness, lack of optimality, low-dimensional planning and navigation-task restrictions, and Time Predictor coverage limitations. v2 explicitly separates logical soundness from dynamic feasibility and adds interpretations of controller compensation and failures under complex dynamics, beyond v1's shorter failure discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds exact OGBench dataset identifiers, controller input/output dimensions, control-frequency settings, additional parameter rows, and a project-page link. It clarifies control timing versus robustness subsampling and the recursive implementation of allocation. Conversely, v1's explicit SafeDiffuser CBF/QP equations and Algorithm 3 are replaced by a prose summary.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.3 positions the framework against four trajectory-stitching works, distinguishing global STL satisfaction from data augmentation and goal-reaching applications. The introduction adopts this positioning, and additional references cover constrained diffusion and time prediction. These substantive additions extend the retained STL-decomposition and diffusion-planning discussion.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the abstract, contribution framing, framework discussion, and conclusion; reorganizes experiments into separate subsections; and moves semantics, decomposition details, task templates, and full Maze2D results into reorganized appendices. This substantially changes the narrative structure beyond simply appending new scientific content.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column layout with wrapped figures and algorithms. Figure 1 is revised; Maze2D results become a partial main-text table and an expanded appendix table with robustness columns. v2 also adds an environment montage and new results tables while relocating and resizing existing illustrations.

improvement.justification: Corrected decomposition rules and explicit conditional soundness arguments address an important gap in v1's correctness justification. Cube, AntMaze, and pipeline evaluations substantially broaden empirical support, while the expanded limitations clarify what logical guarantees and execution results establish. Removing detailed SafeDiffuser pseudocode and equations reduces self-contained reproducibility, and dynamic feasibility remains empirical, but the stronger justification and clearer applicability boundaries provide a substantial overall improvement.
